Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Immunogenicity of Hantavirus and evaluation of vaccine protective efficacy: A comparative neutralizing antibody study of vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains from selected provinces in China.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Statistical analysis Raw data were entered, organized, and analyzed using Excel 2019 and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2. Neutralizing antibody titers were expressed as geometric mean titer (GMT). Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results HV amplification and titer determination To obtain working virus stocks for subsequent neutralization assays, five HV strains (vaccine strains: 84FLi, L99; epidemic strains: SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were resuscitated, propagated, and titrated. All strains replicated efficiently in Vero-E6 cells. On day 7 post-infection, culture supernatants were collected and tested by qRT-PCR, all yielding positive results. IFA revealed typical bright green specific fluorescent granules in infected cells, which were absent in negative control cells, confirming intact viral infectivity (Fig 1). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. All strains formed classical plaques at a 10−3 dilution (Fig 2). The calculated viral titers (PFU/mL) were as follows: 84FLi, 3.08 × 106; L99, 2.25 × 106; SX26, 5.13 × 105; LN03, 1.23 × 104; FJ-17, 1.65 × 106. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control cells. Note: plaque assays were performed in 6-well plates (well diameter: 35 mm). (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Demographic characteristics and HV typing of HFRS patients Among the 48 HFRS patients, 38 were male and 10 were female, with a median age of 53 years. Farmers accounted for 83.33% (40/48) of the cases; the remaining occupations included three students, one worker, one retiree, and three unemployed/homemakers. Among the 28 vaccinees (11 farmers, 11 students, and 6 teachers), 9 were male and 19 were female, with a median age of 31 years. Sera from HFRS patient and vaccinees were all tested positive for HV IgG antibodies. Based on the typing criteria, of the 48 HFRS patient sera, 23 (47.92%) were identified as HTNV infection, 13 (27.08%) were SEOV infection, and the remaining 12 sera were untypable. Inter-individual variation in neutralizing capacity against HV vaccine and epidemic strains Among the 48 HFRS patient sera, 33 showed higher neutralizing titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26, with most differences within 2-fold. Ten sera (20.83%, 10/48) exhibited ≥4-fold higher titers against 84FLi than against SX26. In contrast, neutralizing titers against the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were generally lower than those against the epidemic strain LN03. Nearly half of the sera showed ≥4-fold higher titers against LN03 than against L99. Furthermore, immunogenicity differed between the two SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17; 83.33% (40/48) of sera exhibited higher neutralizing titers against LN03 than against FJ-17. Most sera showed low neutralizing titers against FJ-17, with nearly half (43.75%) having titers <1:20 (Fig 3). analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by hantavirus remains a significant global public‑health burden. Methods: A panel of sera from convalescent patients and vaccinated individuals was tested for neutralizing antibodies against vaccine and epidemic hantavirus strains using an ELISA‑based microneutralization assay. Contribution: The study shows regional hantavirus diversity affects vaccine cross‑protection, underscoring the need for ongoing strain monitoring and vaccine matching. Limitations: Detailed design, power calculations, and longitudinal efficacy data are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒的免疫原性及疫苗保护效力评估:来自中国选定省份的疫苗株与代表性流行株的中和抗体比较研究

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热由汉坦病毒引起,仍然是全球重大公共卫生负担。
analysis_zh.methods: 收集了康复的肾综合征出血热患者血清以及接种双价灭活肾综合征出血热疫苗者的血清,使用基于ELISA的微中和试验测定针对两株疫苗株(HTNV 84FLi、SEOV L99)和三株流行株(HTNV SX26、SEOV LN03、FJ‐17)的中和抗体滴度。

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8+ regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8+ T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8+ Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8+ Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

analysis.summary_en: Background: In HFRS caused by HTNV, CD8+ T cells drive both viral clearance and immunopathology. Methods: Researchers characterized an HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ regulatory T‑cell subset in patients and a murine HTNV model. Results: CD8+ Tregs were reduced in patients, showed a terminal phenotype linked to severity, and two Qa‑1‑binding HTNV peptides were identified; immunization protected wild‑type mice from renal pathology but D227K mice cleared virus better yet suffered more pathology; WT Tregs suppressed effector proliferation via peptide‑specific, TGF‑β‑dependent mechanisms, while D227K altered inhibitory receptor expression and reduced antigen‑specific suppression. Contribution: The study shows HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ Tregs limit immunopathology at the cost of delayed viral clearance, suggesting a therapeutic target for HFRS and similar hemorrhagic fevers. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed methods, sample sizes, and statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis_zh.background: 在由汉滩病毒(汉滩病毒)引起的肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)中,病毒特异性CD8+ T细胞既介导病毒清除,也导致免疫病理。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者在肾综合征出血热患者及小鼠汉滩病毒感染模型中,鉴定了 HLA‐E(小鼠 Qa‐1)限制的 CD8+ 调节性 T 细胞 (Treg) 亚群。
analysis_zh.results: 在患者外周血中,CD8+ Tregs(CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+)显著减少,呈终末分化表型,并与疾病严重程度相关;鉴定出两种能够结合 Qa‐1 的来源于汉滩病毒糖蛋白的九肽;用这些肽免疫可保护野生型小鼠免于肾脏免疫病理,但 D227K knock‐in 小鼠显示病毒清除增强却病理加重;野生型 CD8+ Tregs 通过增加 TGF‐β 分泌,以肽特异性、CD8/TCR 依赖的方式抑制效应 CD8+ 细胞增殖;D227K 突变改变了 Treg 表型,上调抑制受体并降低抗原特异性抑制功能。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现表明,HLA‐E/Qa‐1 限制的 CD8+ Tregs 能在汉滩病毒感染期间抑制免疫病理,可能延缓病毒清除,并提示调控该通路或可为肾综合征出血热及相关病毒性出血热的治疗策略提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未报告详细方法、样本量、统计分析及完整实验数据。

papers.full_text: Disclaimer: Early release articles are not considered as final versions. Any changes will be reflected in the online version in the month the article is officially released. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Dispatch Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany Suggested citation for this article Abstract Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event. Despite being closely associated with human settlements for much of recent human history, brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) were not domesticated as pets until the 17th and 18th Centuries in Japan (1). Wild brown rats, which are prolific synanthropic pests, harbor a great diversity of zoonotic agents (2,3). Pet rats, the domesticated form of brown rats, have likewise been associated with outbreaks of Leptospira spp. (4), Seoul virus (SEOV; Orthohantavirus seoulense) (5), and cowpox virus (6). SEOV is a zoonotic hantavirus found in both wild and pet rats globally (7). In Germany, pet rats have been linked to 4 detections of cases of human SEOV infection (5,8,9). Additional zoonotic pathogens in wild rats include the human pathogenic hepatitis E virus (HEV; Paslahepevirus balayani) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV; Rocahepevirus ratti). HEV is one of the main causative agents of acute hepatitis in humans worldwide and is typically transmitted through the fecal–oral route, consumption of undercooked pork, or blood and organ transplants. rHEV has been detected in wild brown rats and black rats (Rattus rattus) worldwide and is now recognized as a novel human pathogen causing acute and chronic hepatitis (10,11). Rats (Rattus spp.) are reservoirs of rHEV but have also been reported to be incidentally infected with genotype HEV-3 (12). To assess the presence of rHEV, HEV-3, and other related hepeviruses, as well as potential co-infection with SEOV and tissue distribution of hepevirus RNA and SEOV antigen in SEOV-infected and noninfected pet rats, we screened samples from 13 pet rats associated with 3 SEOV detections in human patients in Germany by molecular and serologic assays. Of those 13 pet rats, 11 tested positive for SEOV RNA in previous studies (5,9) (Appendix Table 1). We extracted RNA from liver tissue and screened it by a nested broad-spectrum reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) capable of detecting multiple HEV genotypes and rHEV (Appendix). By sequencing the RT-PCR products, we identified rHEV RNA in 3 of the 13 pet rats (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001), a finding further confirmed by rHEV-specific real-time RT-PCR (Appendix Table 1). The 3 pet rats, which were previously shown to be infected by SEOV (Appendix Table 1), came from 3 different owners; 2 rats were obtained from the same vendor and the source for the third rat was unknown (5,8,9). The 276 nt-long open reading frame (ORF) 1 and corresponding amino acid (aa) sequences of rHEV from the 3 pet rats were nearly identical (99.15%–100%) (Appendix Table 2). For further sequence comparisons and phylogenetic analyses, we downloaded 91 partial and 60 complete genome rHEV sequences from GenBank (Figure). In addition, we determined short ORF1 sequences of 12 wild brown rats from Rotterdam (n = 8) and Amsterdam (n = 4) (the Netherlands) that previously tested positive for rHEV RNA (2). Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 3 pet rat–derived sequences were highly similar (98.55%–98.91%) to a wild rat–derived rHEV sequence from Rotterdam (M226) (Figure, panel A). A multiplex serology approach using bead-based Luminex technology (R&D Systems, https://www.rndsystems.com) (Appendix) detected rHEV-reactive antibodies in 12 of 13 pet rat blood samples; 3 of those 12 samples also showed reactivity to HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1). Subsequent Western blot analysis using the same 2 antigens mainly supported multiplex serology results: 11 of 12 multiplex serology–positive samples also tested positive for rHEV. Of the 11 seropositive samples, 10 also reacted in the Western blot assay with the HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1, Figure 1). That high seroprevalence suggests widespread circulation in pet rat breeding facilities, which should be confirmed using a larger sample size. In all 3 rHEV RNA–positive pet rats, rHEV-reactive antibodies were detected by multiplex serology. Differences in the results of multiplex serology and Western blot assay can be explained by differences in the epitope presentation and sensitivity of both assays. We obtained near-full rHEV genome sequences from the 3 pet rats from Germany (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001) and from 3 of the wild brown rats from the Netherlands by using a combination of high-throughput sequencing and RT-PCR–based sequence determination of the hypervariable genome region. The rHEV full genome sequences from the 3 pet rats were >99.7% identical, and nucleotide and amino acid sequences of all 4 ORFs and encoded proteins were >99.2% identical (Appendix Table 2). As in ORF1, the full genomes from the 3 German pet rats were most similar to the sequence from wild brown rat M226 from Rotterdam (full sequence >99.2% identical; each ORF >98.3%) (Appendix Table 3) and clustered with that sequence in the phylogeny (Figure, panel B). The most closely related rHEV sequences from Germany were detected in wild brown rats from Hamburg (Figure, panel B). The only sequence from a human patient in Germany (13) clustered among sequences from wild brown rats from Berlin, separate from the pet rat sequences (Figure, panel B; Appendix Table 3). On the basis of the complete coding sequences of pet rat–derived rHEV, we selected probe sequences to detect rHEV RNA through in situ hybridization in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues of the pet rats mounted on adhesive microscope slides (Appendix). We clearly detected a disseminated in situ hybridization signal using brightfield microscopy in the livers (hepatocytes) of rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001, confirming the rHEV quantitative RT-PCR results (Appendix Table 1, Figure 2). In addition, we detected an oligofocal in situ hybridization signal in the spleen of pet rat KS22/001 and in the intestinal lumen of pet rat KS19/1354. We detected no signal in the other tissues tested (Appendix Table 4). Nucleocapsid protein immunohistochemistry analysis of the rHEV-SEOV coinfected pet rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001 demonstrated SEOV antigen in multiple organs, predominantly the kidney and brain; antigen was detected less frequently in the spleen, intestine, liver, and lung (Appendix Tables 1, 3, Figure 2). That distribution is consistent with the previously described widespread endothelial tropism of SEOV in naturally infected wild rats and experimentally infected laboratory rats (14). In our study, advanced autolysis limited the assessment of pathological changes. We could not assess colocalization of both viruses because of insufficient tissue material. The co-infection of pet rats with the zoonotic pathogens SEOV and ratHEV and the rat-to-human transmission of SEOV in those cases (8,9) highlights a public health concern posed by pet rats. Unfortunately, the owners of the pet rats did not consent to providing blood samples; therefore, their rHEV serologic status could not be assessed. The near-identical rHEV sequences in the pet rats indicate a single incursion event consistent with potentially being independently obtained from the same vendor in Germany (5). The close similarity between the pet rat rHEV sequences and a wild rat–derived sequence from the Netherlands might indicate a wild rat origin of pet rat rHEV, further circulation by pet rat trade, and (at least mostly) uncoupled dynamics of rHEV in wild and captive rats. Owners and general practitioners should be aware of potential zoonotic risks associated with pet rats so that preventive hygienic measures can be taken and correct diagnosis supported. analysis.background: Pet rats are a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens, including Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV), which have caused human infections in Germany.
analysis.methods: The authors screened samples from 13 pet rats linked to three human SEOV cases using nested broad‑spectrum RT‑PCR for HEV/rHEV RNA, rHEV‑specific real‑time RT‑PCR, and bead‑based Luminex multiplex serology plus Western blot for antibody detection.
analysis.results: rHEV RNA was detected in 3 of 13 rats (≈23%); the three sequences were 99.15‑100% identical and 98.55‑98.91% similar to a wild‑rat rHEV strain from Rotterdam. Serology showed rHEV antibodies in 12 of 13 rats, with most also reacting to HEV‑3 antigen.
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates concurrent SEOV and rHEV infection in pet rats, suggests a single incursion event for rHEV, and indicates widespread circulation of rHEV in pet‑rat breeding facilities.
analysis.limitations: The investigation was limited to a small convenience sample of 13 rats associated with human SEOV cases, and the authors note that larger studies are needed to confirm prevalence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Pet rats are reservoirs of zoonotic pathogens such as SEOV and rHEV, linked to human infections in Germany. Methods: Researchers screened 13 pet rats using nested RT‑PCR, rHEV‑specific real‑time RT‑PCR, and Luminex multiplex serology/Western blot. Results: rHEV RNA was found in 3 rats (≈23%); sequences were >99% identical and closely related to a wild‑rat strain, while antibodies were present in 12 rats, many also reacting to HEV‑3. Contribution: The work shows concurrent SEOV and rHEV infection, suggests a single rHEV introduction, and points to widespread circulation in breeding facilities. Limitations: Small sample size confined to rats linked to human SEOV cases; larger studies are required.

papers.title: An NCG mouse model of Hantaan virus reveals systemic infection and organ-specific cellular tropism.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

full_text_sections.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

papers.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

ANDV has a tripartite negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome in 37 which the S segment encodes the nucleoprotein, the M segment encodes the 38 glycoprotein precursor that gives rise to Gn and Gc, and the L segment encodes the RNA- 39 dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)2. Historical sequencing is uneven across these 40 segments, with many isolates represented by only one or two segments and some M- 41 segment records available only as partial Gn/Gc sequences with separate accessions. 42 ANDV circulates primarily in the long-tailed colilargo (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), with 43 occasional detection in other rodents (e.g. Loxodontomys micropus, Abrothrix longipilis), 44 and repeatedly spill over into humans in Argentina and Chile3,4. The 2018-2019 Epuyén 45 outbreak5 and the 2026 MV Hondius-associated outbreak have therefore raised a central 46 question: are ANDV outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission driven by the 47 recent adaptive viral changes, or by the ecological emergence of pre-existing reservoir 48 lineages already capable of limited human transmission? Previous comparative work 49 proposed candidate mutations associated with person-to-person transmission6, but 50 whether independent outbreaks share a recurrent recent adaptive transition has not been 51 tested systematically. 52 These alternatives make different evolutionary predictions. Under a model of recent 53 adaptive emergence, independently arising human outbreaks should repeatedly be 54 preceded by one or more signatures of viral adaptation. These may include features such 55 as accelerated nonsynonymous evolution, signals of positive selection on outbreak- 56 lineage ancestral branches, convergent amino acid changes, or recurrent perturbation of 57 viral structures involved in entry, replication, immune evasion, or antigenicity. Under an 58 ecological-emergence model, outbreak lineages should instead be distributed across 59 standing reservoir diversity, retain strong geographic structure, and lack a reproducible 60 genomic transition immediately before their detection in humans. 61 For many emerging zoonoses, genomic epidemiology focuses on reconstructing 62 transmission chains after detection in humans. For reservoir-borne viruses, however, the 63 deeper question is often whether the human outbreak lineage can be placed within known 64 animal diversity and whether the branch leading to human emergence shows evidence 65 of accelerated or adaptive evolution. 66 This is particularly challenging for ANDV, for which available genomic data are sparse 67 and unevenly sampled across human and rodent hosts7. Available sequences include 68 known human outbreak clusters, rodent-associated genomes, and ANDV-like sequences 69 that have not always been consistently classified within major clades. Historical isolates 70 are also frequently represented by incomplete segment sets, resulting in substantial 71 differences in sequence availability across segments and sampling dates. These 72 characteristics can complicate molecular dating, as uneven temporal and host sampling 73 can distort the available temporal signal, while incomplete segment sampling and 74 uncertainty in clade classification can influence the inferred phylogenetic structure. 75 . We first reconstruct population-level diversity and introduce a linkage- 82 informed missing-segment framework for retaining sampled viruses in segment 83 alignments when a linked segment is unavailable. We then systematically infer molecular 84 rate estimates, evaluate the presence of time-dependent rate variation across nested 85 datasets and apply the Prisoner of War (PoW) model8 to examine deeper evolutionary 86 timelines of ANDV. Against this macroevolutionary background, we compare the 87 evolutionary emergence of MV Hondius outbreak with four earlier outbreaks involving 88 documented human-to-human transmission: i) a household and nosocomial transmission 89 chain in Southern Chile with five human infections in 2011 (Chile 2011)9 , ii) a three- 90 person transmission cluster in Argentina in 2014 (Argentina 2014)10 , iii) the largest known 91 ANDV outbreak with 34 confirmed infections in Argentina in 2018-2019 (Epuyén 92 2018/19)5, and iv) a two-person family cluster from Chile in 2024 (Chile 2024)11. We then 93 identify the closest sampled relatives and geographic context of each outbreak lineage, 94 reconstruct their evolutionary ancestry, and identify coding substitutions that arose along 95 the ancestral branch leading to each outbreak. By combining these reconstructions with 96 branch-rate, codon-selection, and structural analyses, we directly test whether repeated 97 human outbreaks share evidence of recent adaptive emergence while explicitly 98 accounting for the patchiness of the available genomic records. 99 Results 100 Phylogenetic placement and molecular dating of recorded ANDV human outbreaks 101 To best characterise the broader diversity that ANDV sits in, we first reconstructed 102 maximum-likelihood phylogenies for all publicly available S, M and L genome segments 103 of the Orthohantavirus andesense (Supplementary Figures 1-3). Consistent with 104 previous studies6, the five recorded human-to-human outbreak lineages fell within the 105 four main ANDV clades and were embedded within the broader rodent-associated ANDV 106 diversity. Our expanded curation additionally retains incomplete and partial genome 107 records, including rodent-derived isolates and the Chile 2011 human outbreak 4,9 that 108 would be lost by restricting analysis to complete three-segment genomes, thereby 109 broadening the reservoir context available for each outbreak. The closest sampled 110 relatives of the outbreak lineages were regionally structured. MV Hondius 2026 and Chile 111 2024 clustered within ANDV clade 3, together with rodent-derived (O. longicaudatus) 112 sequences4 and isolated human-infection sequences from Valdivia, Los Ríos, and San 113 . The Argentina 2014 and Epuyén 2018/19 lineages were placed within 117 ANDV clade 2, whereas Chile 2011 fell within clade 1. No human-to-human transmission 118 has been documented yet for members of ANDV clade 4 (which contains the reference 119 ANDV genome, strain Chile-97178692), although it contains genomes derived from 120 isolated human infections. Several rodent-derived sequences fell within ANDV diversity 121 but outside clades 1-4. In particular, two well-supported groups were recovered in M and 122 S segments. Several other isolates also occupied positions outside clades 1-4, but these 123 placements were more weakly supported and/or inconsistent among genome segments. 124 These sequences may represent additional, previously under-recognised lineages of 125 ANDV. We refer to all of these sequences and clusters as “unclassified” (Supplementary 126 Figures 1-3). 127 The nearest sampled relatives of each outbreak lineage differed among genome 128 segments, owing to uneven sequence availability across the segmented genome (Figure 129 1). We refer to these non-outbreak human- or rodent-derived nearest relatives as 130 comparator sequences, because they provide the phylogenetic context for placing 131 outbreak lineages within broader ANDV diversity. The M segment contained the richest 132 set of nearby comparators for all outbreak lineages (total of 78 available ANDV M 133 segment sequences), followed by the S segment (70 available ANDV sequences). full_text_sections.full_text: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks 1 Authors: Charu Sharma1,2*, Sanni Översti1*, Robert Stass3, Alexander G Lucaci4, Jonathan 2 Audet5, David Safronetz5, Lele Zhao2, Katrina Lythgoe1,2,6, Aris Katzourakis1, Thomas A. 3 Bowden3, Spyros Lytras7†, Mahan Ghafari1,2† 4 1Department of Biology, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK 5 2Pandemic Sciences Institute, Nuffield Department of Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford, 6 UK 7 3Division of Structural Biology, Centre for Human Genetics, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK 8 4Department of Systems and Computational Biomedicine, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, 9 NY, United States of America 10 5National Microbiology Laboratory, Public Health Agency of Canada, Winnipeg MB, Canada. 11 6Big Data Institute, Nuffield Department of Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK 12 7Antigen Evolution & Design Lab, Department of Structural Biology and Chemistry, Institut 13 Pasteur, Paris, France 14 *Equal contribution 15 †Corresponding author: S.L. (spyros.lytras@pasteur.fr); M.G. (mahan.ghafari@biology.ox.ac.uk) 16 Abstract 17 Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to- 18 person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence 19 of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal- 20 derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment- 21 linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete 22 genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves 23 isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide 24 states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human 25 outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within 26 geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating 27 detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, 28 while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural 29 mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV 30 Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift 31 attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and 32 ecological opportunity. 33 Introduction 34 Andes hantavirus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and is 35 unusual among hantaviruses in its capacity for documented person-to-person 36 . ANDV has a tripartite negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome in 37 which the S segment encodes the nucleoprotein, the M segment encodes the 38 glycoprotein precursor that gives rise to Gn and Gc, and the L segment encodes the RNA- 39 dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)2. Historical sequencing is uneven across these 40 segments, with many isolates represented by only one or two segments and some M- 41 segment records available only as partial Gn/Gc sequences with separate accessions. 42 ANDV circulates primarily in the long-tailed colilargo (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), with 43 occasional detection in other rodents (e.g. Loxodontomys micropus, Abrothrix longipilis), 44 and repeatedly spill over into humans in Argentina and Chile3,4. The 2018-2019 Epuyén 45 outbreak5 and the 2026 MV Hondius-associated outbreak have therefore raised a central 46 question: are ANDV outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission driven by the 47 recent adaptive viral changes, or by the ecological emergence of pre-existing reservoir 48 lineages already capable of limited human transmission? Previous comparative work 49 proposed candidate mutations associated with person-to-person transmission6, but 50 whether independent outbreaks share a recurrent recent adaptive transition has not been 51 tested systematically. 52 These alternatives make different evolutionary predictions. Under a model of recent 53 adaptive emergence, independently arising human outbreaks should repeatedly be 54 preceded by one or more signatures of viral adaptation. These may include features such 55 as accelerated nonsynonymous evolution, signals of positive selection on outbreak- 56 lineage ancestral branches, convergent amino acid changes, or recurrent perturbation of 57 viral structures involved in entry, replication, immune evasion, or antigenicity. Under an 58 ecological-emergence model, outbreak lineages should instead be distributed across 59 standing reservoir diversity, retain strong geographic structure, and lack a reproducible 60 genomic transition immediately before their detection in humans. 61 For many emerging zoonoses, genomic epidemiology focuses on reconstructing 62 transmission chains after detection in humans. For reservoir-borne viruses, however, the 63 deeper question is often whether the human outbreak lineage can be placed within known 64 animal diversity and whether the branch leading to human emergence shows evidence 65 of accelerated or adaptive evolution. 66 This is particularly challenging for ANDV, for which available genomic data are sparse 67 and unevenly sampled across human and rodent hosts7. Available sequences include 68 known human outbreak clusters, rodent-associated genomes, and ANDV-like sequences 69 that have not always been consistently classified within major clades. Historical isolates 70 are also frequently represented by incomplete segment sets, resulting in substantial 71 differences in sequence availability across segments and sampling dates. These 72 characteristics can complicate molecular dating, as uneven temporal and host sampling 73 can distort the available temporal signal, while incomplete segment sampling and 74 uncertainty in clade classification can influence the inferred phylogenetic structure. 75 . We generated a paired blood- and nasal-derived S, M, and 79 L segment sequence from the outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked 80 collection of public human, rodent, and ANDV-like sequences, including incomplete and 81 partial genomes. We first reconstruct population-level diversity and introduce a linkage- 82 informed missing-segment framework for retaining sampled viruses in segment 83 alignments when a linked segment is unavailable. We then systematically infer molecular 84 rate estimates, evaluate the presence of time-dependent rate variation across nested 85 datasets and apply the Prisoner of War (PoW) model8 to examine deeper evolutionary 86 timelines of ANDV. analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus is unique among hantaviruses for person-to-person transmission, yet it is unclear whether outbreaks arise from recent viral adaptation or pre-existing reservoir lineages. papers.title_zh: 近期人类暴发相关的安第斯病毒谱系的分子进化

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 在 汉坦病毒 中因人际传播而独特,但尚不清楚疫情是源于近期病毒适应还是已有的储存宿主系谱。
analysis_zh.methods: 从 MV Hondius 疫情中获取的血液和鼻腔配对基因组被构建,并与人类、啮齿动物以及不完整安第斯病毒序列的片段关联集合相结合;基于关联信息的缺失片段框架保留了分离株身份和采样时间。
analysis_zh.results: 对五次疫情的系统发育分析将各系谱独立定位于地理结构化的储存宿主多样性中,最近的采样祖先早于检测出现;时间依赖速率分析显示更深的储存宿主历史,且在人际传播前未发现重复的适应性转变。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现将关注点从近期适应转向更深层的系谱特性和生态机会,为安第斯病毒的出现监测提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告

papers.title: Persistent leukopenia masks hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) typically comes with fever, facial flushing, rash, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and leukocytosis. However, atypical manifestations may obscure diagnosis. A 30-year-old man with rodent exposure had high fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia, without overt renal dysfunction despite mild renal involvement in the form of proteinuria. Hantaan virus was confirmed by serology and RT-PCR. The patient recovered following ribavirin and supportive management. This case highlights that in HFRS-endemic regions, hantavirus infection should be suspected among patients with unexplained fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia rather than the typical leukocytosis, even without overt renal dysfunction.

papers.title: Assessing the performance of time series prediction models for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across different high-risk areas in Shaanxi Province, China
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a climate-sensitive disease. Existing forecasting models often overlook prefecture-level variations and environmental drivers. This study compares time series models incorporating environmental factors for prefecture-level HFRS prediction. Methods Monthly HFRS case counts and 14 environmental factors were collected from 2005 to 2023 in four typical prefecture-level cities, including Xi'an, Baoji, Xianyang, and Weinan. Core factors were determined via stepwise screening. We developed four time series models: univariate seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) and long short-term memory (LSTM), alongside their multivariate counterparts with exogenous variables (SARIMAX and LSTMX). Specifically, multivariate models incorporated screened environmental drivers, whereas univariate models relied solely on historical epidemic data. Model robustness was further assessed by rolling-origin validation across three test years (2021−2023), in which the entire modeling pipeline was re-executed within each training window, and the sensitivity of LSTMX performance to the covariate-selection strategy was quantified. Results The predictive value of environmental covariates for HFRS forecasting varied by city and evaluation context. In Xi'an and Baoji, the multivariate LSTMX model showed lower forecasting errors (Xi'an: R 2 = 0.976, RMSE decreased from 69.246 to 17.782; Baoji: R 2 = 0.950, RMSE decreased from 6.694 to 2.805). Conversely, in Xianyang and Weinan, univariate SARIMA yielded lower errors (R 2 = 0.940 and 0.889, respectively), and incorporating covariates did not reduce forecasting errors. Rolling-origin validation across 2021–2023 yielded a consistent ranking: LSTMX had the lowest mean RMSE in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models had lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the screened covariate set was the only strategy that never caused a severe loss of accuracy, whereas including all 14 environmental variables did not reduce errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Pairwise model differences were not statistically significant after Holm correction, and the city ranking changed when the models were refitted on the monthly crude incidence-rate scale; the rankings are therefore reported descriptively and are not interpreted as evidence of regional differences in environmental effects. Conclusions No single forecasting configuration was uniformly optimal across cities: LSTMX with lagged environmental factors yielded the lowest errors in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models yielded lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan; however, these pairwise differences did not reach statistical significance after Holm correction and changed under the incidence-rate scale. When extending these models to new settings, both univariate and covariate-enhanced configurations should be compared.

papers.title: Hantavirus Disease in a Changing World: Reservoir Ecology, Endothelial Dysfunction, Clinical Management, and the 2026 M/V Hondius Andes Virus Outbreak
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses maintained in diverse mammalian reservoirs. Human disease is caused predominantly by orthohantaviruses and manifests chiefly as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia or hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS) in the Americas. Andes virus (ANDV) is epidemiologically distinctive because limited human-to-human transmission has been repeatedly documented. This update-oriented narrative review synthesizes evidence available through to 28 August 2026 and is organized around an integrative framework linking reservoir ecology and spillover, ANDV-specific person-to-person transmission, endothelial and immune dysfunction, clinical phenotype, critical-care management, and One Health preparedness. The recent 2026 M/V Hondius outbreak is used as a case study of how a primarily rodent-borne infection can generate international operational consequences in a mobile, closed setting. Recent HFRS surveillance from Asia and Europe is included to balance the ANDV-focused outbreak analysis. Severe disease is associated with endothelial barrier dysfunction, capillary leak, thrombocytopenia, myocardial or renal involvement, and dysregulated host responses rather than widespread endothelial necrosis. Current evidence supports early recognition and organ support; evidence for ribavirin, immune plasma, monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed vascular therapies differs substantially by syndrome and remains limited or investigational for HPS/HCPS. The M/V Hondius event ultimately involved 13 cases (12 confirmed and one probable) and three deaths, with no further secondary cases after completion of international follow-up.

papers.title: Hantavirus infection and the boundaries of autoimmunity: Vascular immunopathology, autoimmune-like mimicry, and post-infectious phenomena.
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses causing acute systemic vascular syndromes, principally haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although primarily infectious, hantavirus disease may generate vascular, renal, haematological, and systemic phenotypes that overlap with immune-mediated disorders. This Review critically examines the boundary between infection-driven immunopathology and autoimmunity. Hantavirus infection involves endothelial dysfunction, innate antiviral sensing, interferon responses, cytokine and chemokine amplification, complement activation, immunothrombosis, and adaptive immune responses, whose expression is further influenced by virus-, host-, and tissue-specific factors. These mechanisms contribute to the marked heterogeneity of clinical disease and may reproduce autoimmune-like clinical and laboratory features, but do not, in themselves, establish sustained loss of immune tolerance. Current evidence is substantially stronger for acute infection-associated immunopathology and phenotypic mimicry than for persistent autoreactivity or causally attributable post-infectious autoimmune disease.
