analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are rodent‑borne RNA viruses that cause acute systemic vascular syndromes such as haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome.
analysis.main_directions: The review discusses how hantavirus infection triggers endothelial dysfunction, innate antiviral sensing, interferon responses, cytokine/chemokine amplification, complement activation, immunothrombosis and adaptive immunity, generating phenotypes that overlap with immune‑mediated disorders.
analysis.current_state: Evidence strongly supports acute infection‑associated immunopathology and autoimmune‑like mimicry, while sustained loss of immune tolerance or post‑infectious autoimmune disease remains poorly substantiated.
analysis.gaps: Reported autoimmune phenomena are largely case‑based, with limited longitudinal, antigen‑specific and epidemiological data.
analysis.future_research: Further serological, histopathological and mechanistic studies are required to confirm persistent immune dysregulation and to refine diagnostic and therapeutic approaches that separate viral immunopathology from true autoimmunity.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are rodent‑borne RNA viruses causing acute vascular syndromes. Main directions: The review outlines endothelial dysfunction, innate sensing, interferon, cytokine/chemokine storms, complement, immunothrombosis and adaptive responses that mimic immune disorders. Current state: Acute infection drives immunopathology and autoimmune‑like mimicry, but sustained autoimmunity is weakly supported. Gaps: Autoimmune reports are mainly isolated cases with scarce longitudinal and epidemiological data. Future research: Targeted serological, histopathological and mechanistic investigations are needed to verify persistent dysregulation and improve diagnosis and treatment distinction.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒感染与自身免疫边界:血管免疫病理、自身免疫样模仿及感染后现象。

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒是啮齿动物携带的RNA病毒,可导致急性全身血管综合征,如肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述讨论了汉坦病毒感染如何触发内皮功能障碍、先天抗病毒感知、干扰素应答、细胞因子/趋化因子放大、补体活化、免疫血栓形成和适应性免疫,产生与免疫介导性疾病重叠的表型。
analysis_zh.current_state: 证据强有力地支持急性感染相关的免疫病理和类自身免疫的模拟,但持续的免疫耐受丧失或感染后自身免疫疾病的证据仍然不足。
analysis_zh.gaps: 已报道的自身免疫现象主要基于个案,缺乏长期、抗原特异性和流行病学数据。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要进一步的血清学、组织病理学和机制研究,以确认持续的免疫失调,并完善能够将病毒免疫病理与真正自身免疫区分开的诊断和治疗方案。

papers.title: A single-amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and can generate rare outbreaks with person‑to‑person transmission.
analysis.methods: A human ANDV isolate from a person‑to‑person outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same area were compared for lethality in Syrian golden hamsters; genomic sequencing identified nonsynonymous substitutions; the glycoprotein precursor was expressed in human cells to assess Golgi retention and virion‑like particle release.
analysis.results: Sequencing revealed 25 nonsynonymous changes, including a T641I substitution near the glycoprotein cleavage site; both isolates showed similar viral RNA synthesis but the human isolate released virions more slowly; introducing the reciprocal I641T change into the human glycoprotein decreased Golgi retention and accelerated release of virion‑like particles.
analysis.contribution: The T641I change likely represents a human‑adaptive mutation that alters glycoprotein trafficking and enhances virus egress, providing insight into ANDV transmissibility and pathogenesis.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available; detailed methods, sample sizes, and statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus causes HPS and can spread person‑to‑person. Methods: Human and rodent isolates from the same region were compared in Syrian golden hamsters, sequenced, and their glycoproteins expressed in human cells. Results: 25 amino‑acid changes were found, notably T641I; RNA synthesis was similar but the human isolate released virions later, and the I641T revertant showed reduced Golgi retention and faster VLP release. Contribution: T641I may be a human‑adaptive mutation affecting glycoprotein trafficking and virus egress. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided; experimental details and quantitative analyses are missing.

papers.title: Hantavirus Outbreak Caused by Andes Virus Linked to International Cruise Ship Travel - United States, 2026.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV), the only hantavirus known to be transmitted person-to-person, is endemic to areas of South America and can cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, which has a case-fatality rate of approximately 40%. On May 4, 2026, CDC was notified of seven cases of severe acute respiratory illness, including three deaths, among 147 persons aboard a cruise ship in the Atlantic Ocean; the illnesses were later confirmed to be caused by ANDV. No cases occurred among passengers who were U.S. residents. Ten of 28 U.S. resident passengers disembarked before ANDV infection was confirmed aboard the ship. On May 10, the remaining 18 U.S. resident passengers were repatriated to the National Quarantine Unit in Omaha, Nebraska, for risk assessment and monitoring, and where optimized advanced care was available, should symptoms develop. CDC and U.S. health departments monitored 60 additional U.S. residents potentially exposed on flights involving a passenger with symptomatic ANDV infection from the cruise, totaling 88 contacts across 27 jurisdictions. All 88 contacts completed 42 days of monitoring, with no secondary ANDV infections identified. Worldwide, local health authorities assessed and monitored approximately 653 potentially exposed persons from 33 countries. This response highlights the value of rapid coordination among partners to locate and monitor potentially exposed persons during an international outbreak to reduce the risk for ANDV transmission. Prompt notification to public health authorities can facilitate testing, patient care, contact identification, and implementation of measures to limit secondary transmission.

Methods: CDC identified seven severe respiratory cases (three deaths) among 147 cruise‑ship passengers on 4 May 2026, confirmed as ANDV; 18 U.S. residents were repatriated for monitoring, 60 additional U.S. residents and 88 flight contacts were monitored for 42 days, and ~653 exposures were assessed worldwide. analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 (ANDV) 是已知唯一能够人际传播的 汉坦病毒,在南美洲流行,可导致 汉坦病毒肺综合征,致死率约为40%。
analysis_zh.methods: CDC于2026年5月4日收到通知,称在147名邮轮乘客中出现七例严重急性呼吸道疾病病例(其中三例死亡),实验室确认均为ANDV。18名美国居民乘客被遣返进行风险评估和监测,同时卫生部门对另外60名美国居民及来自27个司法辖区的88名航班接触者进行为期42天的监测;全球范围内,相关部门评估了约653名来自33个国家的潜在暴露者。
analysis_zh.results: 七例病例均确认为ANDV感染;美国乘客中未出现病例;在88名受监测的接触者中未发现二次ANDV感染;约653名潜在暴露个体在国际上被追踪。
analysis_zh.contribution: 此次响应凸显了快速协调、接触者识别和监测在国际疫情期间降低二次ANDV传播风险的价值。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要;未报告详细的研究设计、实验室方法、样本量计算和统计分析。

papers.title: Progress in antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus: Current advances and future perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-associated zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), two clinically distinct diseases characterized by vascular dysfunction and potentially severe organ failure. Their geographic distribution, antigenic diversity, and variable clinical outcomes complicate the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. Vaccine strategies are evaluated across regionally implemented inactivated vaccines, DNA candidates assessed in early-phase human trials, and recombinant protein, viral vector, and messenger RNA platforms that remain predominantly preclinical. The review also distinguishes vaccine immunogenicity, experimental protection, durability of immune responses, and clinical effectiveness. Major barriers to translation include virus-specific therapeutic responses, narrow treatment windows, targeted delivery, antigenic diversity, and the absence of validated correlates of protective immunity. This review highlights the experimental and clinical evidence needed to advance promising antiviral and vaccine candidates toward effective strategies for prevention and treatment of hantavirus infections.

The genome comprises small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments that encode proteins required for viral replication and host-cell entry [1]. Rodents are the principal reservoirs of human-pathogenic hantaviruses, and their distribution and transmission are shaped by reservoir ecology and environmental conditions [2]. Ecological analyses based largely on Chinese surveillance further emphasize that environmental variability and host population dynamics can influence hantavirus transmission [3]. Human infection is associated primarily with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), most commonly reported in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas [4,5]. HFRS is characterized by fever, vascular instability, hemorrhagic manifestations, and varying degrees of acute kidney injury [4]. In contrast, HCPS may progress rapidly to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and circulatory shock [5]. These geographic patterns are associated with differences in circulating viral species and their reservoir hosts. Moreover, changes in land use, land cover, and human–rodent interactions may further modify exposure risks [6-8]. Human infection usually follows inhalation of aerosols contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodents, particularly during activities that disturb contaminated materials [9]. Epidemiological investigations have identified residential, occupational, and recreational exposures among patients with HCPS in the United States [10]. Human-to-human transmission is uncommon but has been documented for Andes virus, typically in circumstances involving close or prolonged contact [9,11]. Accordingly, current prevention strategies primarily focus on reducing human exposure to infected rodents and their excreta, particularly in potentially contaminated residential and occupational environments [12]. Vascular endothelial cells are major targets of pathogenic hantaviruses, and clinically significant vascular leakage can develop without extensive direct virus-mediated cytolysis [13]. Altered vascular endothelial growth factor signaling has been implicated in endothelial barrier integrity in experimental systems [14]. Innate and adaptive immune responses contribute to viral control but may also exacerbate inflammation and vascular dysfunction, suggesting that therapeutic strategies may need to address both viral replication and dysregulated host responses [15,16]. Recent surveillance data illustrate the continuing, geographically heterogeneous disease burden. In China, national surveillance recorded 3,271 cases of epidemic hemorrhagic fever and 16 deaths in 2025 [17]. In the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA), 1,885 hantavirus infections were reported in 2023, corresponding to a notification rate of 0.4 cases per 100,000 population [18]. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization reported 229 confirmed cases of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and 59 deaths through epidemiological week 47 of 2025, corresponding to a reported case-fatality proportion of 25.7% [19]. These figures originate from different years, surveillance systems, and case definitions and should not be interpreted as directly comparable estimates of regional incidence or disease lethality. Despite this burden, supportive management remains the cornerstone of clinical care, and no antiviral has demonstrated consistent efficacy across HFRS and HCPS [9]. A randomized clinical trial conducted in China reported reduced mortality and selected complications among patients with HFRS receiving intravenous ribavirin [20]. However, a placebo-controlled trial in HCPS did not establish a clinical benefit during the cardiopulmonary phase, underscoring why treatment findings cannot be generalized across syndromes or disease stages [21]. Favipiravir has shown antiviral activity and improved survival under selected preclinical conditions [22]. RNA interference has suppressed Andes virus replication in cultured cells [23]. Neutralizing monoclonal antibodies have conferred protection in selected animal challenge models, but their efficacy in patients remains unconfirmed [24]. Collectively, these findings illustrate the different levels of evidence supporting current antiviral candidates, ranging from clinical investigation to in vitro and animal-model studies [25]. Prevention faces similar translational challenges. Inactivated vaccines targeting HFRS- associated hantaviruses have been implemented in China [26], while Hantavax is an authorized Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 3 of 23 Narrative Review inactivated Hantaan virus vaccine in South Korea [27]. In contrast, a bivalent Hantaan/Puumala DNA vaccine has reached phase IIa clinical evaluation for safety and immunogenicity, without demonstrating clinical effectiveness against naturally acquired infection [28]. Recombinant protein, viral vector-based, and messenger RNA vaccine platforms have been investigated predominantly in preclinical studies, and the breadth and durability of vaccine-induced protection remain important evidence gaps [29]. Accordingly, the aim of this narrative review is to critically evaluate the molecular rationale, evidence levels, and translational limitations of current hantavirus antiviral and vaccine strategies. The discussion first summarizes mechanisms relevant to therapeutic targeting and antigen design, then compares clinically investigated interventions with preclinical and exploratory approaches, assesses the development status of vaccine platforms, and identifies priorities for further experimental and clinical validation. Virology and pathogenesis of hantavirus Genome organization and viral structure The hantavirus genome comprises three RNA segments, each encoding proteins with distinct roles in the viral life cycle. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA and participates in viral RNA synthesis [1]. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which mediate viral attachment and membrane fusion [30]. Because Gn and Gc contain neutralizing antibody epitopes, they represent important targets for antibody-based interventions and vaccine antigen design [31−33]. Furthermore, the ability of Gn and Gc to self-assemble into virus-like particles in experimental expression systems provides a potential platform for vaccine antigen presentation [34]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is responsible for viral messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication [1]. During transcription, the viral transcription machinery uses short capped RNA primers acquired from host transcripts through cap-snatching to synthesize mRNA from negative-sense genomic RNA (vRNA) [35]. In contrast, genome replication proceeds through primer-independent synthesis of a full-length positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA), or antigenome, from the vRNA template [36]. The antigenome subsequently serves as an intermediate template for producing new negative-sense genomic RNA, rather than functioning as a protein-coding transcript [37]. These mechanistically distinct steps identify RdRp and viral RNA synthesis as relevant targets for direct-acting antivirals. In addition, experimental evidence demonstrating interactions between N and RdRp highlights the importance of the viral replication complex in RNA synthesis [38]. Earlier cell-based studies implicated αvβ3 integrins in entry by certain HFRS-associated hantaviruses [39]. In contrast, protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has been experimentally identified as a critical entry factor for Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus in pulmonary endothelial cells. Disruption of PCDH1 expression also conferred protection against Andes virus challenge in hamsters [40]. For Hantaan virus, clathrin-dependent receptor-mediated endocytosis was demonstrated in a cell-based investigation, although this pathway should not be assumed to operate identically in all hantaviruses [41]. Gn and Gc contribute complementary functions to viral attachment, membrane fusion, and virion assembly [42]. Experimental studies have linked enhanced vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling to increased endothelial permeability [14]. analysis.current_state: Evidence is mixed; some antivirals show promise in vitro or animal models, but human data are limited; vaccines are regionally used or in early trials, with durability and correlates of protection still unclear.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, both severe vascular diseases. Main directions: The review surveys antiviral agents (ribavirin, favipiravir, RNAi, monoclonal antibodies, host‑directed therapies) and vaccine platforms (inactivated, DNA, recombinant protein, viral vector, mRNA). Current state: Evidence is mixed; some antivirals show promise in vitro or animal models, but human data are limited; vaccines are regionally used or in early trials, with durability and correlates of protection still unclear. Gaps: Key uncertainties include narrow therapeutic windows, antigenic diversity, lack of validated immune correlates, and limited clinical efficacy data. Future research: Prospective clinical trials of antivirals and vaccine candidates, longitudinal studies to define protective immunity, and development of broad‑spectrum countermeasures across hantavirus species.

papers.title: Hantavirus: biology, immune responses, and pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise has raised global public health alarms due to its dangerous ability to person-to-person spread. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. Two principal mechanisms, virus-mediated cytopathy and host-driven immunopathology, have been proposed to account for the pathological progression, while their interplay is yet to be fully explored. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease.

papers.full_text: Hantavirus: biology, immune responses, and pathogenesis The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise has raised global public health alarms due to its dangerous ability to person-to-person spread. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease. Facts Paradox of Hantavirus Pathogenesis: Based on current epidemiological and clinical evidence, this review highlights the central paradox of host–pathogen interactions, wherein hantaviruses cause severe immunopathology in humans while maintaining asymptomatic persistent infections in rodent reservoirs. Shift to an Immunopathogenic Framework: To better elucidate the mechanisms of vascular breakdown, this review proposes a transition from a virus-centric model to an immune-mediated framework, systematically integrating early viral IFN-I evasion, excessive CD8+ T cell/NK cell activation, and Treg deficiency. Therapeutic Potential and Research Priorities: While targeted immunomodulators and novel single-dose mRNA vaccines show promise in mitigating severe disease, precise mapping of the receptor-tropism-pathogenesis axis, immune calibration kinetics, and host tolerance mechanisms remains critical for future clinical interventions. Introduction: the central paradox of hantavirus pathogenesis Hantaviruses present a classic paradigm in emerging infectious disease biology, where the central mechanistic puzzle remains fundamentally unresolved: how does a pathogen that establishes persistent, asymptomatic infection in its natural rodent reservoirs trigger severe, frequently lethal immunopathology upon spillover into accidental human hosts? This biological dichotomy sits at the critical intersection of viral molecular biology, host-endothelial dynamics, and immunopathogenesis—domains that have generated competing explanatory frameworks over four decades of research. The two clinically distinct manifestations—hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary/pulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) in the Americas—share an underlying mechanism of endothelial barrier disruption, yet diverge in target organ tropism and severity profiles. The field has oscillated between two dominant explanatory paradigms: a virus-centric model emphasizing direct cytopathic effects and a host-centric model foregrounding immune-mediated vascular damage. Contemporary evidence increasingly favors a synthesis in which viral immune evasion strategies paradoxically amplify subsequent immunopathology, but the precise mechanistic architecture of this interplay remains contested. The urgency of resolving these contested mechanistic details has been underscored by an atypical, high-profile outbreak in May 2026 aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius. This cluster, rapidly traced to Andes virus (ANDV) infection, has renewed focus on the unique biological features of New World hantaviruses—particularly their capacity for person-to-person transmission within closed environments. Here, we synthesize the current scientific literature to map the evolving research landscape on hantaviruses across six key interconnected domains: viral biology and molecular structure, mechanisms of cellular entry and infection, innate and adaptive immune responses, pathogenic mechanisms of vascular leakage, global epidemiological trends, and emerging therapeutic and prophylactic strategies. Viral biology: molecular architecture and evolutionary constraints Genomic organization and structural determinants Structural characteristics of hantavirus and its key proteins. A Schematic representation of the Orthohantavirus Andesense virion structure and genome organization. (Adapted and modified from https://viralzone.expasy.org/11847). B Structure of hantavirus envelope glycoprotein Gc in postfusion conformation in presence of 600 mM KCL (PDB: 5LJX). C High-resolution in situ ANDV single tetramer structure (PDB: 9P3I). D CryoEM structure of Hantavirus ANDV Gn(H) protein complex with 2Fabs ANDV-5 and ANDV-34 (PDB: 8DBZ). Hantaviruses are enveloped negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses within the Hantaviridae family of the order Bunyavirales. The genome contains three segments: the large (L) segment for RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), the medium (M) segment for glycoprotein precursor (GPC, cleaved co-translationally into envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc), and the small (S) segment for nucleocapsid protein (NP)(Fig.1A). This tripartite segmented architecture permits genetic reassortment, conferring evolutionary flexibility that may generate viral variants with novel pathogenic properties. The glycoproteins Gn and Gc are critical determinants of host cell tropism and are the primary targets for neutralizing antibody responses (Figs. 1B – D). The M segment thus occupies a central position in pathogenicity determination: it encodes the molecules responsible for cellular attachment, membrane fusion, and the principal neutralization epitopes. Point mutations in glycoprotein sequences can profoundly alter viral infectivity, as demonstrated by studies showing that two amino acid substitutions in Old World hantavirus glycoproteins are sufficient to generate highly infectious recombinant vectors. The evolutionary stability of these segments is illustrated by real-time genomic sequencing from the May 2026 MV Hondius outbreak cluster. Genomic sequencing and characterisation complemented the epidemiological investigation into the point of origin and subsequent transmission. Each of the S, M, and L genomic segments from the three hantavirus isolates displays high sequence consistency. This observation suggests that the virus has not undergone reassortment, an evolutionary event in which segmented viral strains swap genetic fragments to generate new variants. Accordingly, the virus linked to this outbreak most probably originates from a single genetically stable lineage, instead of arising from recent genetic recombination between distinct hantavirus strains. The RdRp and cap-snatching mechanism The L segment-encoded RdRp mediates both transcription and replication. A distinctive feature of hantavirus mRNA synthesis is the cap-snatching mechanism, whereby the viral RdRp cleaves short capped RNA primers from mRNAs of host origin to initiate viral transcription. This process requires host cell factors, establishing a fundamental dependency on the cellular transcriptional machinery. This host factor requirement for cap snatching represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability, as disruption of this interaction could selectively inhibit viral replication without directly targeting host processes. Host reservoir biology and spillover dynamics Evolutionary distribution, geographic reservoir segregation, and target organ disease phenotypes of major pathogenic hantaviruses. Viral Species Lineage Primary Natural Reservoir Host Vector Family Taxonomy Geographic Distribution Primary Human Clinical Manifestation Target Organ Vulnerability Hantaan virus (HTNV) Apodemus agrarius (Striped field mouse) Muridae Eurasia Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) Renal Glomerular Microvasculature Puumala virus (PUUV) Myodes glareolus (Bank vole) Cricetidae Europe Nephropathia Epidemica (Mild HFRS) Renal Tubules & Epithelial Junctions Sin Nombre virus (SNV) Peromyscus maniculatus (Deer mouse) Cricetidae North America Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS/HCPS) Pulmonary Endothelium & Alveoli Andes virus (ANDV) Oligoryzomys longicaudatus (Long-tailed colilargo) Cricetidae South America Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS/HCPS) Systemic Vasculature & Airway Monolayers Long-term co-speciation within distinct small mammal families ensures persistent, non-lytic asymptomatic carriage in specific hosts. Accidental exposure of the human vascular network to aerosolized excreta from these specific reservoirs determines whether pathology shifts toward Eurasia-centric renal damage or Americas-centric cardiopulmonary syndrome. Each hantavirus species has co-evolved with a specific rodent host reservoir in which persistent, asymptomatic infection is maintained (Table 1). The striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius) serves as the main natural reservoir host of Hantaan virus (HTNV). In European regions, bank voles (Myodes glareolus) act as persistent carriers that preserve Puumala virus (PUUV). The ANDV virus is carried by Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, a wild rodent commonly called the long-tailed colilargo. The geographical range of this species extends from northern Chile and northwestern Argentina where there is a stable population. This rodent is not naturally present in Europe and in the United States, and established wild populations of this species are completely absent abroad. This is crucial since introduction to local rodent populations and potential subsequent rodent-to-human transmission in Europe is not expected. Human infection is accidental, occurring primarily through inhalation of aerosolized virus-containing rodent excreta (urine, feces, saliva). The mechanisms by which reservoir hosts suppress pathology while maintaining viremia—likely involving regulatory T cell-mediated immunosuppression—stand in stark contrast to the hyperinflammatory response in humans. Understanding this dichotomy remains one of the field’s central theoretical challenges. Sustained human-to-human transmission has been validated only for ANDV among hantavirus species. The outbreak on the MV Hondius is considered a case study of a potential superspreader scenario, allowing the effects of prolonged case contact, closed ventilation, delayed symptom appearance and late diagnosis to be studied in a real-life context. All conditions were present to allow secondary cases aboard the ship and tertiary cases across international borders. Mechanisms of cellular entry and tropism Receptor utilization and endothelial tropism Mechanisms of cellular entry and tropism. Schematic depicting hantavirus infection of endothelial cells. Receptor specificity (αvβ3, αvβ1, and PCDH1) drives endothelial tropism. Infection is non-lytic, with viral inhibition of apoptosis promoting persistence. Pathogenesis arises from indirect, immune-mediated endothelial activation and vascular dysfunction, rather than direct cytopathology. (Created in https://BioRender.com). Hantaviruses preferentially target endothelial cells, which constitutes the mechanistic basis for the vascular pathology that defines both HFRS and HCPS. The primary cellular receptors for pathogenic hantaviruses include αvβ3 integrin for pathogenic strains, and αvβ1 integrin for non-pathogenic strains, and latest work identifies PCDH1 as a key receptor governing the cellular entry of New World hantaviruses. This receptor specificity provides a molecular explanation for endothelial tropism and suggests that the tropism itself—rather than any direct cytopathic mechanism—positions the virus to trigger vascular dysfunction through immune-mediated collateral damage (Fig. 2). Non-lytic infection and its pathogenic implications A critical distinguishing feature of hantavirus biology is that infection of endothelial cells is non-cytopathic. Unlike many hemorrhagic fever viruses that destroy target cells directly, hantaviruses establish productive infection without inducing overt cellular damage. This non-lytic character has profound implications for pathogenesis theory: it necessarily redirects pathogenic mechanisms toward indirect, immune-mediated injury rather than direct viral cytopathology (Fig. 2). Furthermore, hantaviruses actively inhibit apoptosis in infected cells, promoting viral persistence and potentially amplifying subsequent immune-mediated damage when cytotoxic responses eventually target infected endothelium. Immune responses: the double-edged sword Immune evasion and immunopathogenesis of hantavirus infection. Hantaviruses enter endothelial cells and replicate with limited cytopathic effect. Early antagonism of type I interferon responses may delay innate immune activation and facilitate viral dissemination. Persistent infection, insufficient immune regulation, exaggerated CD8+/NK cell responses, and complement activation converge to disrupt endothelial barrier integrity, leading to vascular leakage and organ failure. (Created in https://BioRender.com). Hantavirus immunopathogenesis is driven by viral immune evasion and subsequent host immune dysregulation. Suppression of type I interferon signaling by the virus promotes systemic dissemination. Together with regulatory T cell deficiency and hyperactivation of CD8+ T cells, NK cells, and B cells, these cells elicit exaggerated cytotoxic responses, which ultimately cause endothelial damage, complement activation and vascular leakage in severe infections (Fig. 3). Innate immune activation and viral evasion Hantaviruses have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to evade and delay innate immune detection, particularly the type I interferon (IFN-I) response. The IFN-I signaling pathway, mediated through RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), is the primary cellular sensor for hantavirus RNA. However, multiple viral proteins actively antagonize this pathway: the glycoprotein cytoplasmic tail inhibits TRAF3/TBK1-directed IRF3 activation, while the nucleocapsid protein (NP) sequesters double-stranded RNA intermediates to prevent RLR activation. Recent work has identified TRIM25 as a specific target of Hantaan virus immune evasion. HTNV inhibits the type I interferon response by targeting RLR signaling pathways through TRIM25. Furthermore, the glycoprotein and nucleocapsid protein encoded by hantaviruses modulate autophagic flux to suppress the host’s innate immune reactions. By disrupting normal autophagic signaling, these viral proteins suppress IFN-I production and inflammatory cytokine secretion, creating a permissive environment for early viral replication. The theoretical significance of these evasion strategies extends beyond mere immune escape. By delaying the initial innate response, hantaviruses allow greater viral dissemination before adaptive immunity is engaged. When the adaptive response finally mounts, it confronts a more widely distributed infection, necessitating a more vigorous effector response—one that, in the context of endothelial tropism, inevitably causes collateral vascular damage. This “delay-and-amplify” model represents the current leading framework for understanding hantavirus immunopathogenesis. Mononuclear phagocyte redistribution A marked redistribution of peripheral mononuclear phagocytes (MNPs) to the airways occurs during acute Puumala virus (PUUV) infection, which likely drives localized immune activation at the initial infection focus. Pathogenic hantaviruses can replicate within cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS), and this replication capacity has been proposed as a determinant of pathogenicity. The ability to productively infect and disseminate through MPS cells may explain systemic viral spread and the multi-organ involvement characteristic of severe hantavirus disease. Cytotoxic lymphocyte responses: CD8+ T cells and NK cells The adaptive immune response to hantavirus infection is dominated by a vigorous cytotoxic lymphocyte response involving both CD8+ T and NK cells. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) studies in patients with acute PUUV infection have revealed increased numbers of activated CD8+ T and NK cells, along with elevated granzyme A and granzyme B. Critically, the level of this cytotoxic lymphocyte response in pulmonary correlates directly with disease severity and systemic organ dysfunction. The observed link between the magnitude of host immune activation and disease severity represents compelling evidence in favor of the immunopathogenic mechanism. RNA of PUUV was detectable in BAL cellular specimens, with viral loads showing a negative correlation with T-cell-mediated immune responses—suggesting that while effector T cells control viremia, they simultaneously drive tissue damage. NK cell activation is excessive and persistent, with highly elevated numbers persisting in peripheral blood following PUUV infection. Regulatory T cell deficiency Notably, patients with hantavirus infection exhibit reduced regulatory T cell (Treg) relative to healthy individuals. This deficiency in immune regulation may reflect an inadequate counter-regulatory response during acute infection, permitting the unchecked expansion of cytotoxic effector populations. analysis.current_state: Two principal pathogenic mechanisms—virus‑mediated cytopathy and host‑driven immunopathology—are recognized, with hantaviruses antagonising type I IFN and autophagy, leading to exaggerated CD8⁺ T‑cell, NK‑cell and dysregulated humoral responses that damage endothelium.
analysis.gaps: The precise interplay between viral evasion and host immune dysregulation remains incompletely defined, and the receptor‑tropism‑pathogenesis axis lacks detailed mapping.
analysis.future_research: Future work should delineate immune‑calibration kinetics, map receptor‑tropism relationships, and evaluate targeted immunomodulators and single‑dose mRNA vaccines as countermeasures.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The recent Andes virus outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise, notable for person‑to‑person transmission, has heightened global public‑health concern. Main directions: The review covers hantavirus clinical syndromes (HFRS, HCPS), viral entry and immune evasion, host‑driven immunopathology, and current therapeutic/preventive strategies. Current state: Two principal pathogenic mechanisms—virus‑mediated cytopathy and host‑driven immunopathology—are recognized, with hantaviruses antagonising type I IFN and autophagy, leading to exaggerated CD8⁺ T‑cell, NK‑cell and dysregulated humoral responses that damage endothelium. Gaps: The precise interplay between viral evasion and host immune dysregulation remains incompletely defined, and the receptor‑tropism‑pathogenesis axis lacks detailed mapping. Future research: Future work should delineate immune‑calibration kinetics, map receptor‑tropism relationships, and evaluate targeted immunomodulators and single‑dose mRNA vaccines as countermeasures.

papers.title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus (ANDV) is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care. This article addresses eleven practical questions on ICU management, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system. The recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA-ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence. Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology-guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO-capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops.

papers.full_text: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus (ANDV) is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care. This article addresses eleven practical questions on ICU management, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system. The recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA-ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence. Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology-guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO-capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops. Introduction Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) is a rapidly progressive and potentially reversible form of virus-induced endothelial dysfunction characterised by capillary leak-associated pulmonary oedema, distributive shock, myocardial depression, and multiorgan failure. Unlike conventional viral pneumonias, HCPS may progress from a nonspecific febrile prodrome to refractory circulatory collapse within hours. Mortality remains high despite advances in critical care, emphasising the importance of early recognition, physiology-guided resuscitation, and timely escalation towards extracorporeal support. Although this article draws mainly on the Chilean experience with Andes virus (ANDV), most of the supportive intensive care unit (ICU) principles discussed are broadly applicable to severe HCPS caused by other New World hantaviruses. Epidemiology Transmission ecology and pathophysiological determinants of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Panel A illustrates the rodent–environment–human transmission cycle of Andes virus (ANDV). Oligoryzomys longicaudatus is the principal rodent reservoir in Chile and Argentina. Human infection usually occurs after inhalation of aerosolised viral particles. Person-to-person transmission is an ANDV-specific feature and has been documented particularly after close household or intimate contact. Panel B summarises the pathophysiological cascade leading to critical illness. Endothelial activation and dysfunction at the pulmonary capillary level increase vascular permeability, producing capillary leak, acute pulmonary oedema, intravascular hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, and myocardial dysfunction. These overlapping mechanisms explain the rapid development of respiratory failure and mixed shock in severe HCPS. Created with BioRender.com In the Americas, HCPS is predominantly caused by New World hantaviruses, particularly Sin Nombre virus in North America and ANDV in South America. Epidemiological exposure remains a fundamental component of the diagnostic evaluation. Hantaviruses are maintained in persistently infected rodent reservoirs, which shed viruses in urine, faeces, and saliva. Human infection usually occurs after inhalation of aerosolised viral particles from contaminated environments, particularly during rural, peridomestic, forestry, agricultural, or cleaning activities that disturb dust with rodent excreta. Hantaviruses are not arthropod-borne viruses (Fig. 1, panel A). This rodent–environment–human cycle is central to clinical suspicion because exposure may precede the onset of symptoms by days to weeks. ANDV is unique among hantaviruses due to its documented potential for human-to-human transmission, although nosocomial spread remains exceedingly uncommon. Although population-level estimates are limited by scarce data on non-severe cases, hospitalised patients with ANDV HCPS frequently require advanced critical care. In a Chilean cohort of 131 confirmed ANDV cases from 2008 to 2022, approximately 59% were admitted to the ICU, 47% required invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) and 24% required venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support. With contemporary management, mortality among severe ANDV HCPS cases in Chile has decreased substantially, from 60% in the pre-ECMO era to around 25% in recent epidemiological reports and clinical cohorts. Patients with suspected or confirmed ANDV infection should be managed using standard, contact, and droplet precautions, with N95/FFP2 respirators and goggles during aerosol-generating procedures, such as high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), non-invasive ventilation (NIV), and during airway management and similar interventions. Infectious ANDV particles have been detected in respiratory and oral secretions during the acute phase of illness, particularly within the first 2 weeks after symptom onset, when the risk of person-to-person transmission appears to be highest. Therefore, strict infection-control precautions should be maintained throughout this period. Question 1: Why do patients deteriorate so rapidly? Understanding the pathophysiology Natural history of severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The figure depicts the approximate temporal progression of severe ANDV HCPS from exposure and incubation to the prodromal phase, cardiopulmonary syndrome, and recovery. The prodromal phase is followed by an abrupt cardiopulmonary phase, during which patients may deteriorate within hours. Within this phase, circulatory dysfunction may evolve through overlapping vasoplegic/distributive features, capillary leak with intravascular hypovolaemia, and myocardial dysfunction. The lower panel contrasts an untreated or delayed-escalation severe trajectory, associated with high risk of death, with a contemporary managed trajectory characterized by early ICU care, invasive mechanical ventilation when required, timely VA-ECMO consideration, and recovery in survivors. Timeframes are approximate and may vary between patients. Created with BioRender.com The central mechanism of HCPS is an immune-mediated endothelial dysfunction rather than direct viral cytolysis (Fig. 1, panel B). Viral interaction with β3-integrin receptors disrupts endothelial barrier integrity through inflammatory cytokine activation and dysregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The resulting capillary leak produces massive plasma extravasation into the alveolar and interstitial compartments, leading to pulmonary oedema, pleural effusions, haemoconcentration, and severe intravascular hypovolaemia. Simultaneously, myocardial dysfunction may develop, generating an overlapping shock phenotype combining distributive, hypovolemic, and cardiogenic components, with different predominance through the time course of the disease. This pathophysiology explains the rapid haemodynamic deterioration, the deleterious effects of excessive crystalloid administration, and the potential for reversibility with temporary extracorporeal support. The clinical evolution of severe HCPS is summarised in Fig. 2. Question 2: When should I suspect HCPS in a patient presenting to the emergency department or ICU? Bedside red flags for progression to severe HCPS Clinical: Tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnoea, increasing oxygen requirements Laboratory: Falling platelets, haemoconcentration, metabolic acidosis, increasing lactate, proteinuria Imaging: Rapidly progressive bilateral infiltrates, pleural effusions Early diagnosis during the prodromal phase remains critical for survival. Initial manifestations typically include fever, myalgias, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, often without upper respiratory tract symptoms. The coexistence of thrombocytopenia and atypical lymphocytosis should immediately raise suspicion for HCPS in endemic settings or after epidemiological exposure. Bilateral infiltrates in the chest radiographs, progressive hypoxaemia, and disproportionate tachycardia further support the diagnosis. Differential diagnoses include influenza, community-acquired pneumonia, septic shock, leptospirosis, COVID-19, and acute myocarditis. Table 1 presents some clinical criteria used to anticipate progression to severe HCPS. In Chile, when severe ANDV HCPS is suspected, patients are promptly transferred to an ECMO-capable centre. Question 3: What is the initial diagnostic workup, and what are the key findings Chest radiographs initially demonstrate bilateral interstitial infiltrates and septal lines, rapidly progress to diffuse alveolar oedema and pleural effusions, usually with preserved cardiac silhouette size (Fig. 2). Point-of-care ultrasound and echocardiography are valuable for evaluating ventricular function, pulmonary oedema, and haemodynamic phenotype. Laboratory abnormalities commonly include thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, hyponatraemia, elevated levels of lactate, lactate dehydrogenase, transaminases, amylase, B-type natriuretic peptide, and troponin. Definitive diagnosis relies on serological detection of hantavirus-specific IgM antibodies, which are typically detectable at symptom onset. Puumala-based IgM/IgG rapid tests exhibit excellent cross-reactivity, effectively detecting South American ANDV. Reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) performed on buffy-coat samples may improve early diagnostic yield for ANDV infection, particularly before or around the onset of detectable antibodies. The positivity may last for more than two months and can support retrospective diagnosis and genotyping in clusters, although treatment decisions should not be delayed pending molecular results. Diagnostic performance varies according to the assay, timing of testing, and sample type. While rapid serologic assays for hantavirus may show lower sensitivity in early disease (reported around 80–85% in some studies), ELISA-based serology and RT-PCR for ANDV demonstrate substantially higher diagnostic accuracy when performed during the appropriate phase of illness. Importantly, RT-PCR yield is both time- and compartment-dependent: viral RNA detectability varies with the biological fluid tested and declines at different kinetics across blood, respiratory secretions, and saliva. Question 4: How should I perform haemodynamic monitoring? Advanced haemodynamic monitoring is frequently required because circulatory failure in HCPS evolves rapidly (< 24 h) and often combines distributive, hypovolemic, and cardiogenic mechanisms (Fig. 2). Initial haemodynamic assessment should focus not only on arterial pressure but also on tissue perfusion. Bedside evaluation of capillary refill time, skin perfusion, urine output, mental status, and lactate trends provides early evidence of inadequate perfusion and complements invasive monitoring. Continuous invasive arterial pressure monitoring is established early, usually when vasoactive drugs are first required. Persistent hyperlactataemia should prompt reassessment of the underlying shock mechanism. Central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) and the venoarterial carbon dioxide difference (PvaCO2) may provide complementary information regarding oxygen delivery and tissue perfusion but should always be interpreted in the context of the overall macrocirculatory assessment. Bedside echocardiography is our cornerstone of haemodynamic assessment in HCPS because it allows repeated evaluation of ventricular systolic function, preload, and pericardial effusion, while helping identify the transition from distributive or hypovolemic shock to myocardial dysfunction, as shown in Fig. 2. In our practice, all patients admitted to the ICU undergo an initial echocardiographic evaluation followed by serial examinations as their clinical status evolves. Once vasoactive support is initiated, we routinely escalate to continuous cardiac output monitoring using either transpulmonary thermodilution or a pulmonary artery catheter. Both transpulmonary thermodilution and pulmonary artery catheterization allow continuous assessment of cardiac output and filling status, while transpulmonary thermodilution additionally provides measurements of extravascular lung water and pulmonary vascular permeability. This strategy serves several purposes across the disease course: guiding fluid administration against markers of fluid intolerance, detecting the transition from capillary leak–associated hypovolaemia to myocardial dysfunction, identifying patients who require early VA-ECMO consideration, and supporting monitoring during ECMO and weaning. Unlike other forms of shock, advanced monitoring is implemented early because HCPS may progress from capillary leak–associated hypovolaemia to profound cardiogenic shock within a few hours. Consequently, trends in cardiac output and ventricular performance are often more informative than isolated measurements and play a central role in identifying patients who should be considered for early VA-ECMO before irreversible circulatory collapse develops. As myocardial dysfunction evolves, persistently low cardiac output together with normal or increasing filling pressures indicates a shift toward a predominantly cardiogenic phenotype and should prompt timely consideration of VA-ECMO. Question 5: How are fluids and vasoactive drugs administered? Fluid therapy in HCPS represents a therapeutic paradox. Although patients initially develop profound intravascular hypovolaemia due to capillary leak, early fluid administration is required to restore perfusion and limit early organ dysfunction, but administered fluids rapidly redistribute into the interstitial space, worsening pulmonary oedema and pleural effusions. The objective is therefore not fluid restriction per se, but maintenance of adequate preload while avoiding unnecessary expansion of the extravascular compartment. In our practice, much of the cumulative volume is administered within the first 24 h (between 4–6 L), using balanced crystalloids first-line, with albumin as a possible alternative after large crystalloid loads. Following initial fluid resuscitation, further fluid administration is approached with caution, as ongoing capillary leak may preserve apparent fluid responsiveness despite progressive extravascular accumulation. In our practice, we actively monitor fluid intolerance with markers such as rising extravascular lung water with increased pulmonary vascular permeability index, or emerging pulmonary congestion. Consequently, fluid responsiveness alone should not guide repeated fluid challenges. The challenge is not deciding whether the patient requires fluids or vasopressors, but identifying when additional fluid administration becomes more harmful than beneficial as the disease transitions from capillary leak to myocardial dysfunction. Criteria for veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation cannulation in patients with Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome Severe Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome Use of moderate to high dose vasopressors and/or inotropes Arterial lactate > 4.0 mmol/l PaO2/FiO2 < 60 Cardiac arrest Haemodynamic criteria Cardiac index < 2 L/min/m2 despite inotropic support and adequate resuscitation* * Consider the possibility of imminent cannulation if the patient has already been connected to invasive mechanical ventilation Early vasopressor support with norepinephrine is frequently required and should not be delayed while repeated fluid boluses are administered. Beyond restoring arterial pressure, norepinephrine recruits stressed venous volume, increases venous return, and may reduce the need for additional fluid administration. In patients who develop myocardial dysfunction and low cardiac output, inotropic support with dobutamine may be added. However, the need for dobutamine should be viewed as a warning that the disease is evolving towards its myocardial dysfunction phase. It should trigger closer haemodynamic surveillance with serial reassessment of cardiac output and ventricular function. Failure to restore or maintain an adequate cardiac output despite optimised vasopressor and inotropic support identifies patients who should be considered for early VA-ECMO before irreversible circulatory collapse develops. Wernly et al. proposed specific criteria for VA-ECMO cannulation in HCPS, which are shown in Table 2. However, patients meeting these criteria may still not be cannulated because of irreversible multiorgan failure, prohibitive bleeding risk, delayed referral, limited ECMO availability, or goals-of-care decisions. When VA-ECMO is initiated, cautious fluid administration may be required to optimise preload and ensure adequate circuit function during cannulation and early extracorporeal support. Question 6: When, which, and how should respiratory support be provided? Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in HCPS results from increased pulmonary capillary permeability leading to pulmonary oedema. As pulmonary oedema progresses, hypoxaemia and respiratory effort increase, substantially raising oxygen consumption in patients with evolving circulatory dysfunction. HFNC or NIV may be considered in carefully selected patients during the early stages of respiratory failure, provided it does not delay endotracheal intubation in patients with worsening hypoxaemia, increasing work of breathing, or progressive respiratory failure. Given the rapid clinical deterioration that may occur in HCPS, the decision to intubate should anticipate disease progression rather than respond only to established respiratory failure. In this context, endotracheal intubation should generally follow the standard indications for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. However, in HCPS these indications must be interpreted within the framework of a rapidly evolving cardiopulmonary disease, where respiratory failure and circulatory dysfunction frequently coexist. Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology-guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO-capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops. Introduction Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) is a rapidly progressive and potentially reversible form of virus-induced endothelial dysfunction characterised by capillary leak-associated pulmonary oedema, distributive shock, myocardial depression, and multiorgan failure. Unlike conventional viral pneumonias, HCPS may progress from a nonspecific febrile prodrome to refractory circulatory collapse within hours. Mortality remains high despite advances in critical care, emphasising the importance of early recognition, physiology-guided resuscitation, and timely escalation towards extracorporeal support. Although this article draws mainly on the Chilean experience with Andes virus (ANDV), most of the supportive intensive care unit (ICU) principles discussed are broadly applicable to severe HCPS caused by other New World hantaviruses. Epidemiology Transmission ecology and pathophysiological determinants of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Panel A illustrates the rodent–environment–human transmission cycle of Andes virus (ANDV). Oligoryzomys longicaudatus is the principal rodent reservoir in Chile and Argentina. Human infection usually occurs after inhalation of aerosolised viral particles. Person-to-person transmission is an ANDV-specific feature and has been documented particularly after close household or intimate contact. Panel B summarises the pathophysiological cascade leading to critical illness. Endothelial activation and dysfunction at the pulmonary capillary level increase vascular permeability, producing capillary leak, acute pulmonary oedema, intravascular hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, and myocardial dysfunction. These overlapping mechanisms explain the rapid development of respiratory failure and mixed shock in severe HCPS. Created with BioRender.com In the Americas, HCPS is predominantly caused by New World hantaviruses, particularly Sin Nombre virus in North America and ANDV in South America. Epidemiological exposure remains a fundamental component of the diagnostic evaluation. Hantaviruses are maintained in persistently infected rodent reservoirs, which shed viruses in urine, faeces, and saliva. Human infection usually occurs after inhalation of aerosolised viral particles from contaminated environments, particularly during rural, peridomestic, forestry, agricultural, or cleaning activities that disturb dust with rodent excreta. Hantaviruses are not arthropod-borne viruses (Fig. 1, panel A). This rodent–environment–human cycle is central to clinical suspicion because exposure may precede the onset of symptoms by days to weeks. ANDV is unique among hantaviruses due to its documented potential for human-to-human transmission, although nosocomial spread remains exceedingly uncommon. Although population-level estimates are limited by scarce data on non-severe cases, hospitalised patients with ANDV HCPS frequently require advanced critical care. In a Chilean cohort of 131 confirmed ANDV cases from 2008 to 2022, approximately 59% were admitted to the ICU, 47% required invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) and 24% required venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support. With contemporary management, mortality among severe ANDV HCPS cases in Chile has decreased substantially, from 60% in the pre-ECMO era to around 25% in recent epidemiological reports and clinical cohorts. Patients with suspected or confirmed ANDV infection should be managed using standard, contact, and droplet precautions, with N95/FFP2 respirators and goggles during aerosol-generating procedures, such as high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), non-invasive ventilation (NIV), and during airway management and similar interventions. Infectious ANDV particles have been detected in respiratory and oral secretions during the acute phase of illness, particularly within the first 2 weeks after symptom onset, when the risk of person-to-person transmission appears to be highest. Therefore, strict infection-control precautions should be maintained throughout this period. Question 1: Why do patients deteriorate so rapidly? Understanding the pathophysiology Natural history of severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The figure depicts the approximate temporal progression of severe ANDV HCPS from exposure and incubation to the prodromal phase, cardiopulmonary syndrome, and recovery. The prodromal phase is followed by an abrupt cardiopulmonary phase, during which patients may deteriorate within hours. Within this phase, circulatory dysfunction may evolve through overlapping vasoplegic/distributive features, capillary leak with intravascular hypovolaemia, and myocardial dysfunction. The lower panel contrasts an untreated or delayed-escalation severe trajectory, associated with high risk of death, with a contemporary managed trajectory characterized by early ICU care, invasive mechanical ventilation when required, timely VA-ECMO consideration, and recovery in survivors. Timeframes are approximate and may vary between patients. Created with BioRender.com The central mechanism of HCPS is an immune-mediated endothelial dysfunction rather than direct viral cytolysis (Fig. 1, panel B). Viral interaction with β3-integrin receptors disrupts endothelial barrier integrity through inflammatory cytokine activation and dysregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The resulting capillary leak produces massive plasma extravasation into the alveolar and interstitial compartments, leading to pulmonary oedema, pleural effusions, haemoconcentration, and severe intravascular hypovolaemia. Simultaneously, myocardial dysfunction may develop, generating an overlapping shock phenotype combining distributive, hypovolemic, and cardiogenic components, with different predominance through the time course of the disease. This pathophysiology explains the rapid haemodynamic deterioration, the deleterious effects of excessive crystalloid administration, and the potential for reversibility with temporary extracorporeal support. The clinical evolution of severe HCPS is summarised in Fig. 2. Question 2: When should I suspect HCPS in a patient presenting to the emergency department or ICU? Bedside red flags for progression to severe HCPS Clinical: Tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnoea, increasing oxygen requirements Laboratory: Falling platelets, haemoconcentration, metabolic acidosis, increasing lactate, proteinuria Imaging: Rapidly progressive bilateral infiltrates, pleural effusions Early diagnosis during the prodromal phase remains critical for survival. Initial manifestations typically include fever, myalgias, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, often without upper respiratory tract symptoms. The coexistence of thrombocytopenia and atypical lymphocytosis should immediately raise suspicion for HCPS in endemic settings or after epidemiological exposure. Bilateral infiltrates in the chest radiographs, progressive hypoxaemia, and disproportionate tachycardia further support the diagnosis.
